flags.title: Featured Guide
flags.text: This guide has been found to be exceptionally cool by the iFixit staff.

introduction_raw:
This guide will show you how to perform small maintenance techniques on your vehicle that will prolong the life of the vehicle and keep it running in tip-top shape. These include:

* Removing battery corrosion
* Checking and refilling power steering, window washer, radiator, and brake fluid
* Checking and refilling the engine oil
* Checking and adjusting the tire pressure.
introduction_rendered:
This guide will show you how to perform small maintenance techniques on your vehicle that will prolong the life of the vehicle and keep it running in tip-top shape. These include:

  • Removing battery corrosion
  • Checking and refilling power steering, window washer, radiator, and brake fluid
  • Checking and refilling the engine oil
  • Checking and adjusting the tire pressure.

lines.text_raw: Pull on the hood release lever just inside the driver-side door to pop the hood.
lines.text_rendered: Pull on the hood release lever just inside the driver-side door to pop the hood.

lines.text_raw: Locate the hood release latch under the hood. Use one hand to press up on the latch while you lift the hood.
lines.text_rendered: Locate the hood release latch under the hood. Use one hand to press up on the latch while you lift the hood.

lines.text_raw: Insert the hood prop rod into the hole in the hood marked with an arrow.
lines.text_rendered: Insert the hood prop rod into the hole in the hood marked with an arrow.

lines.text_raw: Locate the battery on the left side of the engine bay.
lines.text_rendered: Locate the battery on the left side of the engine bay.

lines.text_raw: If your battery has a cover on it, remove it and set it aside.
lines.text_rendered: If your battery has a cover on it, remove it and set it aside.

lines.text_raw: Before proceeding, identify the positive and negative leads coming off the battery. The negative lead is generally black and may be marked with a "-". The positive lead is often red and may be marked with a "+".
lines.text_rendered: Before proceeding, identify the positive and negative leads coming off the battery. The negative lead is generally black and may be marked with a "-". The positive lead is often red and may be marked with a "+".

lines.text_raw: Never bridge the terminals on the battery with your hands or tools. Shorting the battery can severely injure you.
lines.text_rendered: Never bridge the terminals on the battery with your hands or tools. Shorting the battery can severely injure you.

lines.text_raw: Look for corrosion on the battery terminals. Corrosion can be either white, grey, or blue and will generally be quite noticeable.
lines.text_rendered: Look for corrosion on the battery terminals. Corrosion can be either white, grey, or blue and will generally be quite noticeable.

lines.text_raw: When working with batteries, you must always remove the negative lead from the battery first, even if the corrosion is only on the positive lead.
lines.text_rendered: When working with batteries, you must always remove the negative lead from the battery first, even if the corrosion is only on the positive lead.

lines.text_raw: Using a 10mm hex wrench, loosen the nut on the screw holding the negative terminal in place.
lines.text_rendered: Using a 10mm hex wrench, loosen the nut on the screw holding the negative terminal in place.

lines.text_raw: If the corrosion is preventing you from accessing the nut, use the other (open) end of the wrench or a wire brush to scrape some of the corrosion away.
lines.text_rendered: If the corrosion is preventing you from accessing the nut, use the other (open) end of the wrench or a wire brush to scrape some of the corrosion away.

lines.text_raw: Pull the negative battery cable off of the negative lead.
lines.text_rendered: Pull the negative battery cable off of the negative lead.

lines.text_raw: For this guide, we only show the removal and cleaning of the negative terminal. If you are going to clean the positive terminal, first remove the negative terminal and then remove the positive terminal. The process for removing both leads is the same; it is only the order that is important.
lines.text_rendered: For this guide, we only show the removal and cleaning of the negative terminal. If you are going to clean the positive terminal, first remove the negative terminal and then remove the positive terminal. The process for removing both leads is the same; it is only the order that is important.

lines.text_raw: Scrape the corrosion off of the battery terminal using a wire battery brush or some other scraping/brushing tool.
lines.text_rendered: Scrape the corrosion off of the battery terminal using a wire battery brush or some other scraping/brushing tool.

lines.text_raw: You may want to avoid getting the corrosion all over the inside of the engine bay. Sweeping the corrosion onto a paper plate or rag is a simple way to get the corrosion out of the engine bay without making a mess.
lines.text_rendered: You may want to avoid getting the corrosion all over the inside of the engine bay. Sweeping the corrosion onto a paper plate or rag is a simple way to get the corrosion out of the engine bay without making a mess.

comments.title: Car Maintenance Tips
comments.text_raw:
Just a note. On step 4 it says "Although the corrosion is not bad for the vehicle". That bluish white stuff is powdered Hydrochloric acid, its pretty terrible for your car. A better way of cleaning it off is liberal use of baking soda to neutralize the acid and make sure you wash ALL of it off when you're done.
Also that corrosion is a pretty good indicator of needing a new battery.

lines.text_raw: Re-seat the cable on the negative battery terminal.
lines.text_rendered: Re-seat the cable on the negative battery terminal.

lines.text_raw: Tighten the nut on the battery clamp.
lines.text_rendered: Tighten the nut on the battery clamp.

lines.text_raw: When working with batteries, it is important that you always re-install the negative lead ''last''.
lines.text_rendered: When working with batteries, it is important that you always re-install the negative lead last.

lines.text_raw: Open a packet of battery terminal protector, and, using your finger, coat the (now assembled) battery terminal in a thin layer.  Be sure to cover the outside of both the lead and post, but not to allow any protector between the post and lead.
lines.text_rendered: Open a packet of battery terminal protector, and, using your finger, coat the (now assembled) battery terminal in a thin layer.  Be sure to cover the outside of both the lead and post, but not to allow any protector between the post and lead.

lines.text_raw: Before opening your radiator cap, be sure to let the car cool completely. This may take up to an hour.
lines.text_rendered: Before opening your radiator cap, be sure to let the car cool completely. This may take up to an hour.

lines.text_raw: Twist the radiator cap counterclockwise and remove it from the radiator.
lines.text_rendered: Twist the radiator cap counterclockwise and remove it from the radiator.

lines.text_raw: Fill the radiator with water until you can see the level of water rising in the radiator opening.
lines.text_rendered: Fill the radiator with water until you can see the level of water rising in the radiator opening.

lines.text_raw: A 50/50 mixture of water and coolant is preferable, but plain water is better than nothing. Refer to your owners manual for more instructions.
lines.text_rendered: A 50/50 mixture of water and coolant is preferable, but plain water is better than nothing. Refer to your owners manual for more instructions.

lines.text_raw: Replace the cap on the radiator.
lines.text_rendered: Replace the cap on the radiator.

comments.title: Car Maintenance Tips
comments.text_raw:
You should only be adding pure water if the situation is absolutely dire. If you live in a colder climate and that water in your radiator freezes, your vehicle will be inoperable and you will be looking at a thousand dollars in repair, at least, if not a total loss.

People in warmer climates, where it never hits freezing, often think they can just add water; however, anti-freeze is still preferable, as water will potentially cause rust buildup inside your engine components.

It is very difficult to conceive of a situation in which someone would be unable to go to the store and buy antifreeze.

If you've purchased a used vehicle and you're unsure if it has the correct anti-freeze/water ratio, there are inexpensive tools (approx. $12) you can buy at the parts store which will tell you if its in the correct ratio or not.

Typically a 1:1 ratio, or 50/50, is recommended.

Finally, keep in mind that modern cars often use a specific anti-freeze blend. Almost all cars from before the 90s just use the green stuff.

lines.text_raw: Unscrew the cap from the radiator overflow reservoir located to the left of the radiator, in front of the battery.
lines.text_rendered: Unscrew the cap from the radiator overflow reservoir located to the left of the radiator, in front of the battery.

lines.text_raw: Fill the reservoir with water until the water level is just below the "max" fill line marked on the left side.
lines.text_rendered: Fill the reservoir with water until the water level is just below the "max" fill line marked on the left side.

lines.text_raw: Replace the cap on the reservoir.
lines.text_rendered: Replace the cap on the reservoir.

comments.title: Car Maintenance Tips
comments.text_raw: I wanted to ask if I was losing coolant through my overflow tank cap  as I drove. Would that kill my engine?
comments.text_rendered: I wanted to ask if I was losing coolant through my overflow tank cap as I drove. Would that kill my engine?

comments.title: Car Maintenance Tips
comments.text_raw:
If you lose enough coolant and the engine overheats to the point of failure, usually it will be a total loss on the engine.

However, I've never heard of anyone loosing coolant through the overflow cap.

Rotted hoses or hard pipes, sometimes the water pump (which actually pumps the antifreeze, not water), and a few other locations are the usual suspects for coolant loss.

If you have a blown head gasket, the coolant will mix with the oil and you can slowly lose coolant that way. This problem is usually very easy to diagnose, however.

lines.text_raw: Locate the power steering reservoir near the front right corner of the engine bay.
lines.text_rendered: Locate the power steering reservoir near the front right corner of the engine bay.

lines.text_raw: If the fluid level is below the "Lower Level" fill line, remove the cap and refill the reservoir with power steering fluid.
lines.text_rendered: If the fluid level is below the "Lower Level" fill line, remove the cap and refill the reservoir with power steering fluid.

lines.text_raw: Don't fill the reservoir so much that the fluid level goes above the "Upper Level" fill line.
lines.text_rendered: Don't fill the reservoir so much that the fluid level goes above the "Upper Level" fill line.

lines.text_raw: Locate the dipstick on the right side of the engine.
lines.text_rendered: Locate the dipstick on the right side of the engine.

lines.text_raw: Remove the dipstick from its housing and wipe it off with a rag.
lines.text_rendered: Remove the dipstick from its housing and wipe it off with a rag.

lines.text_raw: Re-insert the dipstick, and then remove it. This will give an accurate reading for the level of oil in the engine.
lines.text_rendered: Re-insert the dipstick, and then remove it. This will give an accurate reading for the level of oil in the engine.

lines.text_raw: The oil level should be between the two dots marked on the dipstick. If the oil level is below the bottom dot, or there is not any oil on the dipstick at all, you will need to add oil.
lines.text_rendered: The oil level should be between the two dots marked on the dipstick. If the oil level is below the bottom dot, or there is not any oil on the dipstick at all, you will need to add oil.

lines.text_raw: Twist the oil filler cap counterclockwise, and remove it from the top of the engine.
lines.text_rendered: Twist the oil filler cap counterclockwise, and remove it from the top of the engine.

lines.text_raw: Using a funnel, pour one quart of manufacturer specified oil into the engine.
lines.text_rendered: Using a funnel, pour one quart of manufacturer specified oil into the engine.

lines.text_raw: Your engine may take different oil depending on the manufacturer specification. Check your owner's manual.
lines.text_rendered: Your engine may take different oil depending on the manufacturer specification. Check your owner's manual.

lines.text_raw: Remove the dipstick and check the oil level.
lines.text_rendered: Remove the dipstick and check the oil level.

lines.text_raw: If the oil level is still low, add more oil.
lines.text_rendered: If the oil level is still low, add more oil.

lines.text_raw: Be sure to not overfill the engine. After adding the first quart, check the oil level every half-quart.
lines.text_rendered: Be sure to not overfill the engine. After adding the first quart, check the oil level every half-quart.

lines.text_raw: When the oil has reached the proper level, replace the dipstick and oil filler cap.
lines.text_rendered: When the oil has reached the proper level, replace the dipstick and oil filler cap.

lines.text_raw: Locate the window washer fluid reservoir in the front right corner of the engine bay.
lines.text_rendered: Locate the window washer fluid reservoir in the front right corner of the engine bay.

lines.text_raw: If the fluid level appears to be low, refill the reservoir with window washer fluid.
lines.text_rendered: If the fluid level appears to be low, refill the reservoir with window washer fluid.

lines.text_raw: You can also use a mixture of water and generic window cleaner, such as Windex. Use a ratio of 5 parts water to 1 part window cleaner.
lines.text_rendered: You can also use a mixture of water and generic window cleaner, such as Windex. Use a ratio of 5 parts water to 1 part window cleaner.

comments.text_rendered: Don't use pure water if you live a cold climate, or it will freeze in the winter and blow out the bottom of the wiper fluid reservoir, or possibly do worse things.

lines.text_raw: Locate the brake fluid reservoir at the rear right corner of the engine bay.
lines.text_rendered: Locate the brake fluid reservoir at the rear right corner of the engine bay.

lines.text_raw: If necessary, unscrew the cap and refill the brake fluid reservoir.
lines.text_rendered: If necessary, unscrew the cap and refill the brake fluid reservoir.

lines.text_raw: Unscrew the valve stem cap from the valve stem on the tire.
lines.text_rendered: Unscrew the valve stem cap from the valve stem on the tire.

lines.text_raw: Using a handheld pressure gauge, check the pressure in the tires. The tires should be inflated to approximately 30 psi.
lines.text_rendered: Using a handheld pressure gauge, check the pressure in the tires. The tires should be inflated to approximately 30 psi.

lines.text_raw: Check your owners manual for the proper tire inflation pressure specific to your vehicle's make, model, and year.
